title: Show the wool
hook: sheep don't show the shepherd their fodder, they show wool (Enchiridion 46)

segments.voice: Yesterday: the quick bather, and the verdict you can't see. Your line was quickly, not badly. What did you describe instead of judging? Day three hundred eighty-one.

Everyone knows someone who just finished a book on mindfulness and can't stop explaining it at dinner, while visibly not being mindful. Maybe we've been that someone. You've been on this path a long time now, nearly four hundred days. It would be natural to want to talk about it. Section forty-six of the handbook has a word for that urge, and then it gives us one of the strangest and most memorable pictures in the whole book: a field of sheep. Today: show the wool.
screen: `EXPLAINING MINDFULNESS AT DINNER.` → `NEARLY FOUR HUNDRED DAYS IN.` → `SHOW THE WOOL.`

segments.voice: First, the rule. Never call yourself a philosopher, Epictetus says, and don't talk much about your principles among people who haven't asked. Do what follows from them. At a dinner, don't explain how one ought to eat. Eat as one ought. Second, Socrates. Epictetus says Socrates had so completely given up showing off that people would come to him asking to be introduced to philosophers, and he would take them. He let himself be overlooked, and didn't mind. Third, the test. When someone tells you that you know nothing, Epictetus says, and it doesn't sting, then you can know you've begun the work. And if talk among people new to all this turns to principles, mostly keep quiet. There's a danger, he says, of throwing up what you haven't digested yet. That's not a polite image. He means it not to be. Fourth, the sheep. Sheep don't bring their grass back up to show the shepherd how much they've eaten. They digest the pasture inside, and what comes out is wool and milk. So, he says, don't show people your principles. Show them the actions that come from digesting them. The point lands softly. Talk is the grass. Practice is the wool. People can't use your grass. They can use your wool: the patience you didn't have a year ago, the gossip you skipped, the promise you kept without swearing. After nearly four hundred days, the best sign of this path may be something someone else notices in you, without you ever mentioning where it came from.
screen: `DON'T CALL YOURSELF A PHILOSOPHER.` · `SOCRATES LET HIMSELF BE OVERLOOKED.` · `DON'T THROW UP UNDIGESTED GRASS.` · `SHEEP SHOW WOOL AND MILK.` · then, large: `SHOW THE WOOL.`

segments.voice: Settle, and breathe. Think back over this path: the words, the stories, the practices. Is there one thing that has actually changed in how you live? Not something you could explain, something you do. A pause before reacting. A smaller portion. A kinder answer. Find it. That's your wool. Now picture using it today, without a word about where it came from. The bell holds the time.
Show the wool. Epictetus: sheep don't bring up grass to show what they ate; they digest it and give wool and milk. Show practice, not principles. Today's word.
Your line: show the wool. Show practice today, not talk: let one thing you've learned show up in what you do, and say nothing about it. Day three hundred eighty-one.

howItsDone: Many people practicing Stoicism avoid calling themselves Stoics or explaining philosophy uninvited, and try to let it show in how they act instead.
